request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Western restaurant server, female, 5th year

[Earlier in the interview]

Interviewee: The year before last, the supervisor post at our Western restaurant was vacant once before. Three people applied. I was one of them, and the other two were Xiao Lin and Ah Mei. In the end the job went to the manager’s nephew. He’d only been here six months and couldn’t even tell one wine vintage from another. When guests asked him, he’d come and ask me. Xiao Lin was later moved to the staff canteen, and Ah Mei was rated unsatisfactory in her appraisal the following year and left not long after. That time, because I was further down the list, the result came out before it was even my turn to be interviewed. The announcement was only posted for one day, and was taken down the next. After that the manager had a talk with me once. He said I was dependable, the floor couldn’t do without me, I should keep up the good work, and there’d be plenty of chances in future. I said OK, thank you.

[Later in the interview]

Interviewer: The supervisor post at your Western restaurant has come up this time. Did you apply?

Interviewee: No, I didn’t. I think things are fine as they are. I’m comfortable doing a server’s job, I know the guests, and lots of regulars ask for me when they come in. Some even get me to keep a table for them. A supervisor has far too much to worry about: rotas, costing, handling complaints, writing reports, and several meetings a month on top of that. It’s not really for me. That’s what I told the manager too. He said he understood, the floor needs experienced people too, and I should keep up the good work. He also said that next time they choose an Outstanding Employee, I’ll be given priority. I feel the same way myself: doing a good job at what I’m doing now is enough, and I don’t necessarily have to move up. If a suitable opportunity comes along in future, we’ll see. The way things are now, it’s quite stable from month to month.
